core_intuitions: Post-training is a load-bearing LADDER: SFT (format/instinct) then DPO (taste) then narrow GRPO (a verifiable skill), each cheaper than the last and a rounding error against the pretraining bill, and each rung depends on the previous one -- skip SFT and DPO has nothing coherent to prefer; skip both and GRPO's reward is 0 everywhere and RL never starts.

Post-training changes what the model DOES (turn-taking, format, taste, one narrow skill), not fundamentally what it KNOWS: SFT and DPO reshape behavior already latent in the base model, and only RLVR adds capability -- and only inside a narrow, verifiable, in-distribution band.

Assistant-only loss masking: only assistant CONTENT tokens plus the closing <|end|> receive gradient (so the model learns to STOP); the system/user turns and the <|assistant|> role marker are context the model conditions on but is not trained to emit -- and the mask must land on the TARGET position after the causal shift, the single most common SFT bug.

DPO reshapes response log-probabilities RELATIVE to a frozen reference: push the winner up and the loser down; the intractable partition term appears in both and cancels in the difference (no reward model, no rollouts), and beta~0.1 is the KL leash -- with the notorious failure mode being BOTH rewards falling while the loss, which only sees the difference, still drops.

GRPO's group-relative advantage: a group of G sampled responses IS the critic -- standardize the verifier's rewards within the group into a z-score advantage and broadcast that single scalar to every token of the response (terminal reward, no per-token credit assignment); a PPO-style clip lets you reuse the rollouts for a few gradient steps.

The cold-start trap: RL produces gradient ONLY from mixed-outcome groups; an all-wrong or all-right group has zero std, zero advantage, and zero gradient, so the base+SFT model must already succeed roughly 10-40% of the time -- which is exactly why the RLVR task must be narrow and in-distribution at 100M.

new_figures.name: posttraining-ladder-100m
new_figures.concept: The three-stage post-training ladder (SFT then DPO then narrow GRPO): what each rung teaches, its objective and cost, what machinery it deletes versus full PPO-RLHF, and why the ordering is load-bearing.
new_figures.rationale: This is the spine of the entire chapter -- the 'ladder is load-bearing and ordered' thesis is stated in the intro, the cost table, the ASCII pipeline block, and the closing section. The chapter's only current visual for it is a weak monospace ASCII arrow-chain. A single infographic that fuses the ladder metaphor to fuse the four things the reader must hold together (teaches / objective / cost / what-it-deletes) turns the chapter's central argument into one glanceable picture and is the highest-leverage figure here.
new_figures.placement: Section '## Where post-training fits, and what it costs at 100M' (anchor the marker where the monospace base-model -> SFT -> DPO -> GRPO pipeline block currently sits, replacing it as the section's visual).
new_figures.brief: A three-rung ASCENDING ladder / staircase read bottom-left to top-right, each rung a labeled stage box, with a faded PPO-RLHF comparison tower on the right. START node at the base: 'Base model (Ch. 14.8): fluent text CONTINUER -- has knowledge and fluency, but does not take turns, follow instructions, or stop.' RUNG 1 SFT, arrow from base: title 'SFT -- teaches FORMAT & INSTINCT'; sub 'see a user turn -> produce an assistant turn -> STOP'; objective chip 'assistant-masked cross-entropy'; cost chip '~0.5-2 A100-hr'; output label 'chat model'. RUNG 2 DPO, arrow up: title 'DPO -- teaches TASTE'; sub 'prefer chosen over rejected'; objective chip 'Bradley-Terry logistic on implicit reward, frozen SFT reference'; cost chip '~0.5-2 A100-hr'; output 'aligned chat model'; a small red-strike tag 'deletes: reward model + rollouts'. RUNG 3 GRPO/RLVR, arrow up to the top: title 'narrow GRPO/RLVR -- teaches a VERIFIABLE SKILL'; sub 'be correct on NEW inputs, graded by a program'; objective chip 'group-relative clipped surrogate + KL leash'; cost chip '~2-6 A100-hr'; output 'narrow-skill model -> agent (Ch. 14.10)'; strike tag 'deletes: the critic'. On the RIGHT, a greyed/faded tall tower labeled 'full PPO-RLHF (deliberately avoided)' stacking four blocks: reward model, policy, value/critic net, frozen reference -- with the reward-model and rollout blocks and the critic block visibly crossed out by the DPO and GRPO rungs respectively, and a caption 'what remains is exactly what our budget affords.' BOTTOM BANNER spanning the width: 'each rung cheaper than the last (a rounding error vs the pretraining bill) and each is LOAD-BEARING: skip SFT and DPO has nothing coherent to prefer; skip both and GRPO's reward is 0 everywhere and RL never starts. Post-training changes what the model DOES, not what it KNOWS.' Also annotate the three rungs collectively with 'each answers a different question: FORMAT / TASTE / SKILL.' Constraints: the A100-hr and data figures shown are the chapter's own illustrative ranges (do not invent new benchmark numbers); use the theme's semantic accent for the active ladder and a muted/neutral fade for the avoided PPO tower (no hardcoded primary colors); everything inside the viewBox with clear bottom-to-top reading order and no overlapping chips; must be legible in both light and dark themes.

new_figures.name: sft-assistant-mask-stackml
new_figures.concept: Assistant-only loss masking on the concrete Stack-100M ChatML template: which tokens are supervised (assistant content + closing <|end|>) versus context (everything else), and that the mask lands on the target position after the causal shift.
new_figures.rationale: The chapter calls the masking boundary 'the single most common SFT bug' and devotes a full subsection, a warning callout, and two explicit design decisions (supervise the closing <|end|> to learn to stop; mask the <|assistant|> marker) to it. This is an inherently visual, per-token idea currently carried only by prose and code comments. A labeled token ribbon over the chapter's own rendered example makes 'what gets a gradient' unmistakable and directly prevents the bug the chapter warns about.
new_figures.placement: Section '### Assistant-only loss masking and why it matters' (anchor the marker right after the heading, near the loss equation).
new_figures.brief: A horizontal token RIBBON of the chapter's own single-turn rendered conversation, in reading order, wrapping to two rows if needed, with each cell tagged by its supervision mask. Cells in order: <|bos|> | <|system|> | [You are Stack-100M, a concise, honest assistant.] | <|end|> | <|user|> | [What is 17 times 4?] | <|end|> | <|assistant|> | [17 times 4 is 68.] | <|end|> | <|eos|>. Encode mask=0 CONTEXT (conditioned on, NO gradient) as muted/neutral cells: bos, the system role marker, system content, its <|end|>, the user role marker, user content, its <|end|>, the <|assistant|> role marker, and the trailing <|eos|>. Encode mask=1 SUPERVISED (receives gradient) as the theme's positive accent: ONLY the assistant CONTENT tokens ('17 times 4 is 68.') AND the closing <|end|> of the assistant turn. Two callout annotations with leader lines: (1) on the assistant's closing <|end|>: 'SUPERVISED -- learn to STOP. Mask this and the model never gets gradient to end its turn: the never-shuts-up failure.' (2) on the <|assistant|> role marker: 'MASKED -- the harness emits it to cue generation; the model learns what comes AFTER it, not to emit it mid-turn.' BELOW the ribbon, a small 'causal shift' strip: a short row of input tokens t_i with arrows to their targets t_{i+1}, showing the mask applied to the TARGET position, and masked targets replaced by 'IGNORE (-100)' which F.cross_entropy skips. Caption under it: 'the mask lands on the TARGET after the shift -- masking before the shift, or marking <|assistant|> as supervised, silently trains on the prompt. This boundary is the single most common SFT bug.' A tiny legend: filled = supervised (in loss), muted = context (conditioned on only). Constraints: only the small illustrative content shown (no invented numbers); positive accent vs neutral must be clearly distinguishable in both themes; keep the long content strings inside their cells (truncate visually if needed) with no overflow in dark theme; single static frame, everything inside the viewBox.

new_figures.name: dpo-relative-reshaping
new_figures.concept: DPO moves response log-probabilities RELATIVE to a frozen reference -- push winner up and loser down (the margin) -- and its notorious failure mode where both rewards fall together while the loss, which sees only the difference, still drops.
new_figures.rationale: DPO's whole intuition is relative, not absolute, and the chapter hammers two things a static picture nails: the implicit-reward margin (winner-up/loser-down against the frozen reference, with the partition term cancelling) and the failure where 'both chosen and rejected log-probs fall.' The prose worked example gives exact small magnitudes to anchor a figure. No figure currently shows the two-outcome contrast that tells a practitioner their DPO run is silently degrading.
new_figures.placement: Section '### The DPO loss, briefly (full derivation in Ch. 5.7)' (anchor the marker after the DPO loss equation, before the implementation subsection).
new_figures.brief: Two side-by-side panels sharing a vertical axis 'response log-prob relative to the FROZEN reference (= implicit reward / beta)', with a dashed horizontal baseline at 0 labeled 'frozen SFT reference pi_ref'. In each panel show two markers: y_w (winner / chosen) and y_l (loser / rejected), starting on the baseline (policy == reference: both log-ratios ~0, margin 0, loss = -log 0.5 = 0.693 nats, acc = coin flip) drawn faint, and their moved positions drawn solid with arrows. PANEL A titled 'What DPO should do (correct)': winner arrow UP, loser arrow DOWN; bracket the vertical gap between them as 'margin = beta*(winner log-ratio - loser log-ratio)'; annotate with the chapter's magnitudes 'winner +3 nats, loser -1 nat -> margin = 0.1*4 = 0.40 logit -> sigma(0.40) ~ 0.60'; label 'chosen reward UP, rejected reward DOWN.' PANEL B titled 'The notorious failure': BOTH winner and loser arrows point DOWN, but the winner falls LESS than the loser, so the difference still grows; annotate 'loss only sees the DIFFERENCE -- it drops while BOTH rewards collapse and the model gets worse. Diagnostic: chosen_reward must trend UP, not just the margin.' A note strip spanning both panels: 'the intractable partition term beta*logZ(x) appears in BOTH winner and loser and CANCELS in the difference -> no reward model, no rollouts, a static set of pairs. beta ~ 0.1 is the KL leash: even a 4-nat separation is only a 0.4-logit margin -> small, deliberate steps.' Constraints: use ONLY the chapter's own illustrative magnitudes (0.693, 3, -1, 0.40, 0.60, beta 0.1); encode up/positive and down/negative with the theme's semantic hues (no hardcoded primaries); the two panels must be clearly distinguishable and the 'both fall' vs 'split apart' contrast legible at a glance in both themes; single static frame, no overlaps, inside the viewBox.

new_figures.name: grpo-group-advantage-arith
new_figures.concept: GRPO on the concrete arithmetic task: sample a group of G completions, grade each with the exact-match verifier, standardize rewards within the group into z-score advantages, broadcast the single scalar to every token -- and the cold-start trap where only mixed-outcome groups produce gradient.
new_figures.rationale: This fuses the chapter's two most important RLVR intuitions -- the group-IS-the-critic standardization and the cold-start / mixed-outcome requirement that decides whether RL works at 100M at all -- onto the chapter's OWN worked example (17*4, R=[1,0,1,0,0,1,0,0], advantages +1.29 / -0.775). It is anchored in the concrete task and the '####' verifier, so it is distinct from the Part-V deep-dive figures and is the payoff visual for the section titled 'making RL actually work at 100M.'
new_figures.placement: Section '### GRPO advantage and loss (full derivation in Ch. 5.8)' (anchor the marker after the advantage equation; it also serves the '### The task and the verifier' and the worked-example callout).
new_figures.brief: A left-to-right pipeline over the chapter's arithmetic worked example, plus a cold-start band underneath. STEP 1 PROMPT: a cell 'Compute 17 * 4. Give the final integer after ####' with a small tag 'gold = 68'. STEP 2 GROUP of G=8 sampled completions stacked vertically, each a short response chip ending in '#### <n>', each tagged by the exact-match verifier as correct or wrong using render-safe marks (filled check / hollow cross, NOT tofu-prone unicode), with the chapter's outcomes R = [1,0,1,0,0,1,0,0] -- 3 of 8 correct (37.5%, labeled 'in the RLVR sweet spot'). Draw a horizontal 'group mean R-bar = 0.375' line across the reward column and note 'std ~ 0.48'. STEP 3 STANDARDIZE: show A_hat_i = (R_i - mean)/(std + eps) as bars on a zero line -- correct samples at +1.29 (up), wrong samples at -0.775 (down); annotate 'more wrong than right, so each correct sample is pushed up harder than each wrong is pushed down -- the group self-balances.' STEP 4 BROADCAST: take ONE correct completion and one wrong completion and stamp EVERY token cell of each with its response's single scalar (all +1.29 up-arrows / all -0.775 down-arrows); caption 'RLVR gives every token the same terminal reward -> one scalar advantage per response, broadcast to all its tokens (no per-token credit assignment).' COLD-START BAND across the bottom: three mini group thumbnails -- (a) all wrong (0,0,0,0...): mean 0, std 0 -> every A_hat = 0 -> gradient meter EMPTY, label 'too HARD -- no gradient'; (b) mixed (like the main example): variance -> gradient meter FULL, label 'sweet spot ~10-40% -> LEARNS'; (c) all right (1,1,1,1...): mean 1, std 0 -> every A_hat = 0 -> meter EMPTY, label 'too EASY -- no gradient'. Band caption: 'RL climbs only from the VARIANCE within a group: the base+SFT model must already succeed SOMETIMES. This is why the task must be narrow and in-distribution at 100M -- the cold-start trap.' Constraints: use ONLY the chapter's own illustrative values (G=8, R=[1,0,1,0,0,1,0,0], 0.375, ~0.48, +1.29, -0.775, and 0/1 rewards in the band); no invented benchmark numbers; correct/wrong and positive/negative advantage encoded with the theme's semantic hues (no hardcoded primaries); the empty-vs-full gradient meters in the cold-start band must be distinguishable at a glance in both themes; no overlaps, clear left-to-right then top-to-bottom reading order, everything inside the viewBox; single static frame conveys the whole pipeline.

summary: A concept-rich capstone chapter with ZERO figures, so this is a foundational-figure build, not an audit. Its central argument is the load-bearing three-stage LADDER (SFT -> DPO -> narrow GRPO), and it teaches three distinct mechanisms in depth: assistant-only loss masking, DPO's relative log-ratio reshaping, and GRPO's group-relative advantage with the cold-start trap. I propose four static figures, one for the spine and one per mechanism, each anchored in THIS chapter's concrete 100M artifacts (the Stack-100M ChatML template, the DPO worked-example magnitudes, the 17*4 arithmetic group R=[1,0,1,0,0,1,0,0]) so they complement rather than duplicate the Part-V deep-dive figures. Priorities: posttraining-ladder-100m (1) replaces the weak ASCII pipeline and fuses teaches/objective/cost/deletes; sft-assistant-mask-stackml (1) makes the 'single most common SFT bug' unmistakable on a labeled token ribbon; grpo-group-advantage-arith (1) is the payoff visual fusing standardization + broadcast + cold-start on the chapter's own example; dpo-relative-reshaping (2) contrasts the correct winner-up/loser-down move against the both-rewards-collapse failure. All four are single-frame comparisons -- no animation needed; motion would add nothing the static frames do not already carry.
